sections.title: Appearance and features
sections.text: A small Gymnopilus with an ochre-brown to rusty-brown fruit body, dry and matte. In Holec's collections the cap is 0.5–1.2 cm across (other descriptions report up to about 2.4–3 cm); it starts nearly hemispherical or conico-convex and becomes convex to almost flat. Its surface is finely tomentose, not hygrophanous, and not translucently striate. The ventricose gills are attached to the stem; Holec describes them as rather distant, while Corriol describes closer gills in the Pyrenean collection. They change from rusty ochre to dark rusty brown at maturity. The slender, cylindrical, fibrillose stem is about 1.5–3 cm tall and has white tomentum at the base.

sections.title: Habitat and ecology
sections.text: This wood-decaying fungus is reported chiefly on strongly decayed conifer stumps, especially spruce (Picea) and fir (Abies), in natural or semi-natural montane forests. Fruiting bodies may grow in small groups, sometimes within cavities in rotten wood. Published records include summer and autumn; they do not establish a universal fruiting season.

sections.title: Taxonomy and identification
sections.text: Gymnopilus josserandii is the name accepted by the taxonomic references consulted. Holec treats the historical names Naucoria subsphaerospora and Gymnopilus subsphaerosporus as invalidly published. The spores are small, subglobose to broadly ellipsoid, about 4.5–6 × 3.5–4.8 µm, and finely verruculose; the gill-edge cystidia have a distinctive narrow-necked, rounded-head shape. Microscopy may be needed for species-level identification: colour and host wood alone are insufficient, and related Gymnopilus can look similar.

sections.title: Food status and caution
sections.text: The food status of this species has not been assessed in this entry. Do not eat a mushroom based on a photograph or these descriptive characters alone; misidentification among wood-growing mushrooms can have serious consequences.

traits: Ochre-brown to rusty-brown cap, dry, matte and finely tomentose; usually small, though reported size varies
Attached, ventricose gills, rather distant to closer depending on collection, rusty ochre then dark rusty brown when mature
Slender cylindrical fibrillose stem, with white tomentum often present at the base
Grows chiefly on strongly decayed conifer stumps, especially spruce and fir
Subglobose to broadly ellipsoid, finely verruculose spores; microscopic traits help distinguish the species
safetyNote: Food status not assessed. This description cannot validate a foraged specimen or recommend its consumption; seek expert identification.
